title: Bioactive Restorative Materials to Preserve and Help Rebuild Compromised Tooth Structure
html:
Written by: Robert A. Lowe, DDS

INTRODUCTION

Prolonging the functional lifespan of teeth and helping to maintain the patient’s dentition for their entire lifetime….is that not the mission of all restorative dentistry? The need for dental restorations made with artificial “tooth-like” materials results from prolonged contact between bacterial metabolic byproducts (acids) and the tooth surface, which demineralize enamel and dentin, leading to tooth decay and the ultimate destruction of healthy tissue. This process is a well-established fact. It makes sense that early diagnosis of dental caries, micro-preparation (instrumentation), and restoration with materials that interact with the tooth in the oral environment in such a way that inhibit this cycle and prolong (or eliminate) the need for more advanced restoration, or tooth loss, should be the “manifest imperative” of all restorative dentists. However, as a profession that often “watches” this disease process progress under the premise of “being conservative,” we can often defeat this ultimate goal. Is it possible for “smart” dental materials to help prolong restorative success, and thereby tooth longevity? After all, there is no such thing as a “permanent” restoration that can last a lifetime.

Key Causes for Dental Caries and Restoration Failures

Repairing dental caries with direct or indirect restorative materials creates a tooth-restorative interface (margin), or gap, that becomes the “weakest link” (other than occlusal forces) influencing the restoration’s longevity. According to Murray and others1,2 as many as 70% of all restorations are replacements for previously failed restorations. Three different factors can account for the majority of these replacement restorations.

  1. Bacterial Dysbiosis. The oral microbiome is comprised of gram-positive microorganisms, such as Streptococcus mutans, whose biproducts of metabolism are very acidic (low in pH). Bacterial dysbiosis can cause a decrease in pH in close proximity to the tooth surface, leading to decalcification (loss of calcium and phosphate ions) resulting in incipient or recurrent tooth decay.
  2. Marginal Failure and Microleakage. The restorative margin also provides an opportunity for damage from bacterial metabolic byproducts. Bacteria, whose diameter is less than 1 µm, can aggregate in marginal gaps, which can be as small as 17 to 20 µm. This can lead to microleakage at restorative margins accelerating the potential for failure of the restoration. Bulk fill flowable composites and composite warming devices, such as Compex HD (AdDent) that decrease the viscosity of paste composites prior to placement in the cavity preparation, can help decrease potential microleakage that can be caused by layering or inadequate adaptation to the cavity walls due to the viscosity of the material.
  3. The Biofilm. A sticky proteinaceous film comprised of microorganisms, extracellular matrix polysaccharides (sugars), glycoproteins, and nucleic acids produced by the microbes that covers tooth and restorative surfaces. If not mechanically removed by toothbrushing and flossing, biofilm increases bacterial acid contact with tooth and restorative surfaces, severely reducing the life of the restoration and ultimately the tooth.3,4,5

How Bioactive Dental Materials Can Help Prevent Restorative Failures

In addition to fluoride’s effect on healthy hydroxyapatite, which makes enamel less susceptible to demineralization from the acid byproducts of bacterial metabolism, a material’s ability to release calcium and phosphate ions to help rebuild demineralized dentin represents a new paradigm for preventing and reducing the recurrence of dental caries. These new “smart” bioactive dental materials react to pH changes in the oral environment, triggering changes in both the material and the tooth. Hence, “biomineralization” refers to the exchange of calcium and phosphate ions within the tooth substance, forming new hydroxyapatite and, in many cases, repairing existing demineralized hydroxyapatite. Bioactivity may also facilitate the precipitation of hydroxyapatite crystals on the material surface in the presence of moisture (saliva). This phenomenon has the potential to aid in the sealing of restoration margins for extended periods of time due this mineral-like deposition at the tooth-restorative interface…a built-in “interface defense system” can help margins remain sealed and decrease the deleterious effects of microleakage.6,7,8

Bioactive dental materials can also actively interfere with the colonization of bacteria on the surface of restorations by the release of therapeutic ions which neutralize acids raising the pH thereby reversing the deleterious effects of demineralization, and by modifying surface properties to interfere with or prevent microorganisms from adhering and forming a mature biofilm.9 Having restorative materials that can protect, as well as repair and help seal the marginal gap that exists around all dental restorations, can help preserve the natural tooth and extend the life of dental restorations. They are particularly useful for patients with high caries indices, where controlling the problem can be difficult. Acidic oral environments can cause extensive tooth damage, especially if a patient doesn’t know which end of the toothbrush has the bristles!

In this article, we will examine how bioactive restorative materials, such as ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow (Pulpdent Corporation), are used in clinical settings to restore posterior occlusal and proximal lesions.10 The patient, a 57-year-old male, presented with decay diagnosed by radiograph on the distal surface of tooth No. 29. A preoperative occlusal view of tooth No. 29 is shown in Figure 1. Figure 2 shows the DO cavity preparation and sectional matrix placed prior to restoration. Note the precise adaptation of the sectional matrix band and ring (Strata-G Sectional Matrix [Garrison Dental Solutions]) to the proximal walls of the cavity preparation. When using a flowable restorative material, it is very important not to have any gaps where overhangs could potentially occur during placement and curing of the composite. These areas can be difficult to remove with rotary instrumentation while maintaining physiologic contours. Next, perform a total etch of the preparation with 37% phosphoric acid for 10 seconds, followed by thorough rinsing with water from the air-water syringe. After air-drying, ensuring the dentin is not over-desiccated. Next, the bonding resin is applied using a micro brush (Figure 3); the adhesive is air-thinned while the solvent evaporates, then light-cured for 20 seconds according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The restorative process begins with applying ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow into the cavity preparation. The dual-cure mixing tip has a cannula that can be easily bent to create the proper angle for easy access to the gingival aspect of the proximal box. ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow is then delivered to the preparation in one bulk increment (Figure 4). The viscosity is such that the material readily flows and accurately fills the entire preparation with intimate adaptation to the cavity walls. The ability of the material to “self-level” helps limit the potential of overfilling the cavity preparation during placement. Next, the material is light-cured based on the manufacturer’s instructions. Unlike layered paste-type composite materials that can be sculpted to their final shape, flowable materials must be shaped, for the most part, with rotary instrumentation after light curing. Therefore, it is important not to overfill or overbulk the material when filling the cavity preparation. After marking the occlusion with articulating paper, detail the anatomic form using a fine, bullet-shaped composite finishing carbide bur (Figure 5). Polishing the restoration is accomplished with rubber abrasive wheels (A.S.A.P. All Surface Access Polishers [Clinician’s Choice]). Figure 6 is an occlusal view of the completed restoration.

As previously mentioned, when using a flowable composite restorative material, accurate placement of the proximal matrix can mean the difference between achieving good proximal contours and contacts and struggling to refine these areas with rotary instrumentation after placement of the material and light curing. Figure 7 shows a case of “back-to-back” premolars prepared for MOD composite restorations. Tooth No. 5 has sectional matrix bands and diamond wedges (Bioclear Matrix Systems) placed proximally. When placed, the unique design of diamond wedges adapts the sectional matrix to the concavities of the preparation (gingival margin) preventing overhangs from flowable composite extending over the preparation margins due to inadequate seal. Most conventional wedges do not adequately seal gingival margins when concavities are present. Since proximal contact will be made with tooth No. 4 when it is restored, a ring is not needed at this time when restoring tooth No. 5. Again, it is important to point out that the matrix is precisely adapted to the vertical walls of the preparation. The preparation is not overfilled beyond the proximal height of the matrix band. It is also important to mention that the sectional matrix band should not extend occlusally beyond the proposed height of the restored marginal ridge to avoid excessive rotary adjustment of the composite after placement. After placing the sectional rings, it was noticed that the matrix edges did not adapt well to the cavosurface margins of the preparation. This situation could lead to excess flowable composite material at the interproximal cavosurface margins that would result in overhangs and poor proximal contours. To prevent this, Teflon tape is used to fill the gaps between the rings and matrices, pushing the matrix material into contact with the preparation margins (Figure 8). Figure 9 is an occlusal view of the completed MOD ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow restorations on tooth Nos 4 and 5.

ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow can also be used as a dentin replacement to fill large cavity preparations in one bulk increment, then use a packable composite to complete the occlusal portion of the restoration. Figure 10 shows a preoperative view of a large, failing multi-surface composite on tooth No. 31. After removal of the existing composite and recurrent decay, the preparation is shown from an occlusal view (Figure 11). The bucco-lingual width of the mesial proximal box will make it difficult for many sectional matrix and ring systems to adapt and create proper proximal contour. An extra-wide sectional ring is used (Strata-G Wide Prep Ring [Garrison Dental Solutions]) to properly adapt the vertical portion of the sectional matrix to the cavosurface margin of the preparation, avoiding indentation of the matrix (Figure 12). The preparation is etched with 37% phosphoric acid for 10 seconds, then rinsed and air-dried. After application of bonding resin, the material is light-cured for 20 seconds per manufacturer’s instructions. Once the adhesive steps have been completed, ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow was placed and cured on both proximal aspects of the preparation to rebuild the vertical walls and marginal ridges of the Class II portion of the restoration. A matrix was not used on the distal aspect since 1) there was no adjacent tooth present, and 2) placement of a matrix could cause bleeding contamination from the adjacent gingival tissues. Any minor overextension of the composite material can be corrected with rotary instrumentation after light curing the material, thus preventing contamination of the adhesive surface during placement (Figure 13). Now, all that remains is to restore the Class I portion of the restoration. ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow can be used as a dentin replacement to fill the majority of the preparation, leaving about 1 to 2 mm of space to use packable material to sculpt the morphologic occlusal surface of the restoration. Figure 14 shows the segmental placement of packable composite to recreate the occlusal surface morphology. At a subsequent appointment, a DO restoration was completed on tooth No. 29 using ACTIVA BioACTIVE Bulk Flow (Figure 15).

CONCLUSION

Clinical cases have been shown demonstrating the use of a bioactive bulk-fill restorative material to restore initial carious lesions and to replace defective restorations that have failure due to marginal breakdown and recurrent caries. Using materials that have the potential to extend the life of the restoration due to biomimicking benefits inherent in the material itself provides a benefit to the life expectancy of the tooth and the long-term dental health of the patient.11

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Dr. Lowe graduated magna cum laude from Loyola University School of Dentistry in 1982. Upon graduation, he entered private practice, as well as teaching as an associate professor in operative dentistry at Loyola until its closure in 1993. In 2000, he relocated his practice to Charlotte, NC. In January of 2021, Dr. Lowe joined the faculty of MUSC James B Edwards College of Dental Medicine and is currently an associate professor in the Department of Reconstructive and Rehabilitative Services, while continuing to maintain part-time private practice as an associate at Charlotte Dental Arts in Charlotte, NC. Dr. Lowe lectures internationally and publishes in well-known dental journals on aesthetic and restorative dentistry. He is a clinical evaluator of materials and products with many prominent dental manufacturers. Dr. Lowe received fellowships in the AGD, ICD, ADI, ACD, ASDA, and received the 2004 Gordon Christensen Outstanding Lecturers Award. In 2005, he was awarded Diplomat status on the American Board of Aesthetic Dentistry. He is a consultant for a number of dental manufacturer’s worldwide. He can be reached at boblowedds@aol.com.

Disclosure: Dr. Lowe received an honorarium from Pulpdent Corpration.
